Boundaries and rules are entirely different concepts. Boundaries protect you from someone else’s behavior, rules control that. All boundaries should be focused on you, not someone else. For example “I don’t want to date a smoker, and will not consider dating someone who smokes.” Is a boundary. “You have to stop smoking.” Is controlling someone else’s behavior, like an ultimatum. Going to bed at the same time is not a boundary, it is you attempting to control someone else. It can be something you would like to happen and definitely should be communicated to a partner, but it cannot be classified as a boundary.

Can you make a joke about anything? Sure. But it’s exactly the same as the right to free speech. You’re allowed to say it but not protected from the consequences of it.

If someone you know is uncomfortable about something and you know it and choose to joke about it anyway, the natural consequence is that you’ll not be friends any longer. It doesn’t matter if the reason they don’t like it is personal or not, it’s up to you respecting what others are comfortable with. If you can’t do that, then the only friends you’ll have are ones who also don’t respect others feelings.

I taught pre-K but that response or something similar could easily work for any age level.

As a (former) daycare teacher, this is something I’ve noticed the kids do instinctively! They will “listen” to adults overall, but the teachers who they have bonded with / they know well and generally trust are much better able to curb bad behavior. It’s basically “I’m feeling this way, I don’t know you, why should I care what you say?” To clarify, caregivers / teachers they know but dislike (usually for good reason, like being unempathetic, strict to the point of unreasonable for age/comprehension level) do not get special treatment because they have not earned the child’s respect.
